request.rawInput: How did the German assurance of support relate to Austria-Hungary's diplomatic posture during 4–10 July 1914?

scope.interpretedQuestion: How did the German assurance of support relate to Austria-Hungary's diplomatic posture during 4–10 July 1914?
inclusions: Franz Joseph's appeal for German backing
Vienna's reported ultimatum posture by 10 July
the disputed relationship between assurance and posture
exclusions: a complete account of the July Crisis

presentation.title: The German Assurance and Vienna’s Posture, 4–10 July 1914

synthesis.text: In the days after the Sarajevo assassination, Austria-Hungary sought to know how far it could count on German backing before deciding how to respond to Serbia.

Franz Joseph sent a personal letter with Szögyény, framing the assassination as Pan-Slavist aggression that threatened both empires alike — the appeal that accompanied Austria-Hungary’s request for backing.
On 5 July, Ambassador Szögyény met with Wilhelm II in Berlin and reported back to Vienna that Germany had promised its full support.

Vienna’s leadership, including Foreign Minister Berchtold, was informed of this assurance on or shortly after 5 July — though the exact hour it was received is not established from the surviving record.

By 10 July, German Ambassador Tschirschky reported from Vienna that Austria-Hungary was preparing demands on Serbia designed to be difficult to simply accept — and that Wilhelm II, reading this report, dismissed the value of further diplomatic consultation.

Historians disagree about how much the German assurance actually drove what followed: some read it as part of deliberate German encouragement toward war, others see the outcome as shaped by contingent choices distributed across several capitals, not by Berlin’s intent alone.

findings.label: Szögyény reported a German assurance of full support.
Vienna’s posture by 10 July was reported as resistant to easy acceptance.
The causal influence of the assurance remains disputed.

entities.description: German Emperor; gives the verbal assurance of support and later annotates Tschirschky’s 10 July report.
Austro-Hungarian Emperor; sender of the personal letter Szögyény delivered to Wilhelm II.
Austro-Hungarian Foreign Minister; recipient of Szögyény’s telegram; his ultimatum-planning posture is reported by Tschirschky on 10 July.
Austro-Hungarian Ambassador to Berlin; delivers Franz Joseph’s letter and reports Wilhelm II’s assurance in telegram no. 237.

claims.statement: Franz Joseph’s letter framed the Sarajevo assassination as the result of Pan-Slavist agitation aimed at weakening the Triple Alliance and destroying Austria-Hungary, seeking German backing on that basis.
Szögyény reported that Wilhelm II stated Austria-Hungary could count on Germany’s full support.
Wilhelm II reacted to Tschirschky’s 10 July report by dismissing the value of further diplomatic consultation, quoting Frederick the Great against councils of war.
By 10 July 1914, Vienna’s diplomatic posture, as reported by Tschirschky, was oriented toward demands not designed to be simply accepted.

passages.excerpt: Characterizes Fischer’s thesis: German leaders "planned a war of aggression" from late 1912 onward, reducing the interpretive weight placed on the international system.

passages.excerpt: Characterizes Clark’s The Sleepwalkers as "saturated with agency," focused on "how" rather than "why," reading German behavior as relatively calm through the crisis and distributing causal weight across multiple powers’ contingent choices.
passages.locator: Keiger, "The Historiography of the Origins of the First World War" (2016)

passages.excerpt: Franz Joseph writes that the Sarajevo assassination was "the direct consequence of the agitation carried on by the Russian and Serbian Pan-Slavists whose sole aim is the weakening of the Triple Alliance and the destruction of my Empire."
